meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Whiskey Is for Drinking; Water Is for Fighting Over'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Mark Twain. The earliest instance located to date is a UPI wire headline of 22 May 1982 that credits him with no source — 72 years after he died.

answer.label: Not Mark Twain — an anonymous Western adage
answer.authorDates: Earliest instance located May 1982 · author never identified
answer.sourceLine: No printed page, manuscript, letter or speech in Twain’s work has ever been produced for this line. The earliest instance Quote Investigator ↗ could locate is a South Dakota newspaper of 12 April 1983, where it was already being used as an unattributed saying; a UPI wire headline of 22 May 1982 antedates that and already credits Twain, with no source given — 72 years after he died.

source.excerpt: Whiskey is for drinking; water is for fighting over.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ dates the earliest instance it could locate to the Aberdeen American News of Aberdeen, South Dakota, 12 April 1983, where a government-agency head used the line without attributing it to anyone. QI concludes that substantive support for linking the saying to Twain is non-existent and suggests the adage be designated anonymous, while noting that its April 1983 cite can probably be antedated.

It can. A UPI wire story by Robert Crabbe out of Sacramento, on California’s Proposition 9 canal fight, runs under the headline “Whiskey Is To Drink. Water Is To Fight Over” — Mark Twain ↗, dated 22 May 1982 in UPI’s archive — eleven months before QI’s earliest cite of any kind. It moves the paper trail, not the verdict: 1982 is still 72 years after Twain died, the headline names no source, and Twain appears nowhere in the reporter’s copy beneath it. That is a wire-desk flourish, not a citation.

Barbara Schmidt’s TwainQuotes.com ↗, the standard online index of sourced Twain quotations, carries the line with a single-sentence verdict: it has been attributed to Twain, but until the attribution can be verified it “should not be regarded as authentic.”

Wikiquote ↗ lists it in the Misattributed section, calling the attribution likely apocryphal and noting that it is not listed at all in either R. Kent Rasmussen’s The Quotable Mark Twain (1998) or David W. Barber’s Quotable Twain (2002).

Guy Rocha, former Nevada State Archivist, wrote that Twain did not say it in any version, and reported that researchers at the Mark Twain Papers and Project at UC Berkeley’s Bancroft Library “have found nothing to support the claim” — Myth #122, Nevada State Library and Archives ↗.
source.excerptNote: There is no original context to quote, because no original has been found. Quote Investigator transcribes the April 1983 wording as “Whiskey is for drinking and water is for fighting,” spoken by a government-agency head and, in QI’s reading, already functioning as an anonymous adage; the familiar “water is for fighting over” form appears in a Montana natural-resources journal that same summer, which is where QI first records the Twain credit — though a UPI headline had already made it in May 1982.
source.rightsNote: No author and no first publication have been identified, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for the wording. The saying is not public domain by virtue of sounding old: the earliest printing located so far is a 1982 wire story, itself still within copyright, and the phrase’s ultimate origin remains unknown.

author.name: Mark Twain
author.heading: Why it sticks to Twain
author.bio: Samuel Langhorne Clemens, writing as Mark Twain, was an American humorist, novelist and lecturer who spent the early 1860s in Nevada and built much of his early reputation on the mining West. That biography is exactly why a dry-country wisecrack about water rights sounds like him — and why it isn’t. Twain is among the most heavily misattributed writers in English: unsigned aphorisms drift toward his name the way they drift toward Churchill’s or Einstein’s, and researchers at the Mark Twain Papers and Project have found nothing tying this one to him.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is a rare case where the misattribution is better documented than the quote. The saying has no known author, so it has collected famous ones — plus a date that nobody can source.

items.why: Twain died in 1910; the earliest instance Quote Investigator ↗ could find is from 1983, and it carries no author. Barbara Schmidt’s TwainQuotes.com ↗ lists the line only to warn that it “should not be regarded as authentic,” and Wikiquote ↗ places it under Misattributed, noting it appears in neither of two standard Twain quotation reference works.

Former Nevada State Archivist Guy Rocha found the Florida League of Cities website crediting Will Rogers with “Whiskey is for drinking and water is for fighting” — the same line, a different folksy American humorist, and no more evidence than the Twain version has. See Myth #122 ↗.

Rocha recorded a site that dates the whiskey-and-water line to 1884 “but does not tell us where it came from” — a precise-looking year attached to nothing. Dates like this are how a bare attribution acquires false authority. Nevada State Library and Archives ↗.

A federal agency’s own Arizona-centennial page ↗ on mid-century water disputes credits the saying to Twain and offers no citation — a reminder that official provenance is not the same as verified provenance.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody has produced an author. Quote Investigator ↗ expects its April 1983 citation can eventually be antedated and invites better references — a UPI headline of May 1982 already does, and it names no author either. Push the date back as far as you like; until someone produces a source, the honest label is anonymous, which is precisely what QI recommends.

context.heading: A water-law slogan, not a Twain line
lead: Every early citation sits in the same world: Western water policy. The earliest instance located anywhere is a UPI wire headline of 22 May 1982, on California’s Proposition 9 canal fight; the 1983 South Dakota appearance came from a government-agency head; the first Twain credit QI located ran in a Montana natural-resources journal that summer; a Wall Street Journal piece followed in September 1983; and in March 1984 Arizona Governor Bruce Babbitt put a version of it into a U.S. House hearing, according to Quote Investigator’s citation trail ↗. The saying reads like folk wisdom because that is functionally what it is — a compact argument for how seriously the arid West takes prior-appropriation water rights.

The Twain credit is a plausibility error rather than a forgery. He lived in Nevada in the early 1860s and wrote the West as comedy, so a dry-country wisecrack slots neatly under his name. Guy Rocha, writing for the Nevada State Library and Archives, noted that people fighting water wars across the American West simply love to use the quote, and that hundreds of websites hang it on Twain regardless — including, he found, one that dates it to 1884 without saying where the date came from.
detailsBody: 22 May 1982 — UPI wire, Sacramento. Robert Crabbe’s story on California’s Proposition 9 canal fight runs under the headline “‘Whiskey Is To Drink. Water Is To Fight Over’ — Mark Twain.” Outside QI’s trail and eleven months earlier than it. The Twain credit is in the headline only; the copy beneath never names him.

12 April 1983 — Aberdeen American News, South Dakota. QI’s earliest located instance, spoken by a government-agency head named Warren Neufeld and, by QI’s reading of the context, used as an anonymous adage. No Twain, no author at all.
Summer 1983 — Western Wildlands: A Natural Resource Journal, Montana. The first appearance QI records that credits Mark Twain, and the first in the now-familiar “water is for fighting over” form.
September 1983 — Wall Street Journal. Credited to Twain again, in a shortened wording.

1984–85 — the saying goes national. A U.S. House hearing (Governor Bruce Babbitt), the New York Times, the San Diego Union, a Resources for the Future annual report and the Philadelphia Inquirer all carry it — sometimes credited to Twain, sometimes attributed only to “Westerners” in general.
context.pull: “Somebody surely made it up and we don’t know who.” — Guy Rocha, former Nevada State Archivist

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator finds no substantive evidence Mark Twain said or wrote the saying; its earliest located instance is the Aberdeen American News (Aberdeen, South Dakota), 12 April 1983, spoken by government-agency head Warren Neufeld as an anonymous adage; the first Twain credit and the 'water is for fighting over' form appear in Western Wildlands (Montana), Summer 1983; the Wall Street Journal used it in September 1983; Arizona Governor Bruce Babbitt used a version at a U.S. House hearing in March 1984; further 1984-85 citations in the New York Times, San Diego Union, Resources for the Future and Philadelphia Inquirer; Twain died in 1910; QI says antedating is probably possible and suggests the adage be designated anonymous.

UPI's archive carries a wire story by Robert Crabbe, SACRAMENTO dateline, on California's Proposition 9 (the Peripheral Canal) ahead of the 8 June 1982 primary, headlined "'Whiskey Is To Drink. Water Is To Fight Over' -- Mark Twain", with datePublished 1982-05-22 (a duplicate second-day entry carries 1982-05-23). This antedates Quote Investigator's earliest located instance of any kind (April 1983) by about eleven months and its earliest located Twain credit (Summer 1983) by about a year. The Twain credit is headline-only: Twain is named nowhere in the article body, so it is a wire-desk attribution with no source, 72 years after Twain died.

TwainQuotes.com (Barbara Schmidt) lists 'Whiskey is for drinking; water is for fighting over.' with the note that it has been attributed to Mark Twain but until the attribution can be verified the quote should not be regarded as authentic; the same page carries a genuine sourced whiskey passage from Life on the Mississippi.

Wikiquote's Mark Twain page lists 'Whiskey is for drinking. Water is for fighting over.' under the Misattributed section, stating the attribution seems likely apocryphal, that it is not listed as authentic on Twainquotes, and that it is not listed at all in either Rasmussen's The Quotable Mark Twain (1998) or David W. Barber's Quotable Twain (2002); the page also gives Twain's dates as 30 November 1835 - 21 April 1910, American humorist, novelist, writer and lecturer.

Guy Rocha, former Nevada State Archivist, states Mark Twain did not say the phrase in any version; that researchers at the Mark Twain Papers and Project at UC Berkeley's Bancroft Library have found nothing to support the claim; that 'somebody surely made it up and we don't know who'; that one website credits Twain in 1884 without saying where it came from; that the Florida League of Cities website credits Will Rogers with the saying; and that Twain lived in Nevada in the early 1860s.

A U.S. Bureau of Reclamation Arizona-centennial page about mid-20th-century Arizona and Western water disputes attributes 'Whiskey is for Drinking, Water is for Fighting' to Mark Twain and provides no date or source for the attribution.
The Center for Mark Twain Studies runs 'The Apocryphal Twain', a series addressing quotations habitually misattributed to Mark Twain; it does not contain a post on this particular saying.
